title: How do you build your game?

posts.author: Eternidade_1
posts.body:
Let's say you're going to build a game by yourself, where would you start?
- Story
- Inspiration from a game (fan game)
- Setting (game scenario maps)
- Music (Establishing emotion and feelings as a priority)
- Systems (Searching for scripts, plugins or event systems)
- Gameplay (Where you create as you play, adapting the game for the best performance)
In addition, you need to create your own images, using an editing tool. So which images would be a priority to start with?
- Characters (original characters for the game's setting)
- Icons (Establishing all the points that will be explored in the future.
- Backgrounds and parallax (Exploring the concept of the background for the entire game)
- Big pictures and busts of characters (To express dynamic dialogues on the game screen)
- Tilesets (Performing maintenance and adaptation for the game maps)
- Animations (Exploring variety to cause visual effect beyond standard battles)
How do you build your game?
Among other aspects, such as sound selection or color palette, which I did not mention in this post.
I would really like to know your recipe for completing a project.

posts.author: Pixelbird14
posts.body:
I suggest going in this order for ideas: (first to last)
Inspiration from a game (fan game)
Setting (game scenario maps)
Story
Systems (Searching for scripts, plugins or event systems)
Gameplay (Where you create as you play, adapting the game for the best performance)
Music (Establishing emotion and feelings as a priority)
But that's just my preference.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body: I start with mechanics and how I want the game to play. The type of graphics I need depend on how the game plays. If it's a 2D sidescroller I only need sideview graphics, top-down I need 4 direction graphics, if there is diagonal movement I may need 8 directions, etc. Once I have mechanics made I can easily use them as the base for a lot of potential games in different settings, etc.

posts.author: alice_gristle
posts.body:
Step 1: I have a story idea for Game A. I write a synopsis.
Step 2: I think of cool graphics for this game. I make a tileset. I try to make some portraits, but
Step 3: I have an idea for Game B. It's only a title. I jot it down.
Step 4: I start mapping for Game A. I make all the maps.
Step 5: I have an idea for Game C. I write a synopsis.
Step 6: I also write a scenario and start rough draftin' a script for Game C.
Step 7: I have an idea for Game D. I write a short premise.
Step 8: I try out colour palettes for Game D.
Step 9: I write a scenario and a script for Game A.
Somewhere down the line, I combine Game B and Game D into an entirely new game. Then I bury Game A 'cuz the story doesn't work. Years pass and I work on various games in the afore-described fashion. Then I dig out Game A again, rework it as a cute li'l puzzle game, and put out.
Usta be a time when I was hella guilty and ashamed that I work like this, but now I'm like, well, if this is the way I hafta work, so be it. Haphazardin' it and goin' strogg

posts.author: Jollo
posts.body:
I haven't finished a RPG Maker Game yet but I think the very first thing you need is a storyidea (for a story driven game ofc). With that idea usally also comes the idea for the setting. So you then know what kind of mood the graphics should have and so on.
With that you can start building your characters. And while you write the story you could also start building a prototype. Testing tilesets (do they fit the mood), try out dialogues and so on. I think it's very important to try and test very early on to see if it will work out. Sometimes you get new ideas while building a prototype.

posts.author: TRIDIUM
posts.body:
Any way you like it, honestly.
With Dime A Dozen, I started with characters, than story, than setting and gameplay .
MSSESBSAF grew from an idea I had about combing areas and items, and than I used a character design I liked.
So yeah, whatever you want, really. Generally, leave art and music for last, but hey, if that's what you're good at, go ahead.

posts.author: teleshock_p
posts.body:
I'll add the disclaimer that I only ever finished one project.
1. I have a vague idea like "A murder mystery game with catgirl maids in a cat café".
2. I write down as much as possible about the story, setting, characters and locations.
3. I try to decide if I could actually create it. Is it too complex? Are there too many characters to write and draw portraits for? Are there too many locations to map?
4. I draw some character sprites, some portraits and some environmental tiles.
5. I create a single map mock-up in RPG Maker.
At that point I can decide whether it's going anywhere. If I decide to stop working on it, then I will look if I could maybe repurpose any good parts for another project.
Also: I don't have experience with parallax mapping, but I think that's something that would come last. Parallax maps might look fancier than tileset based maps, but if during testing people complain that your maps are too big, too small or too confusing then I suspect it would be easier to change a tileset based map than a parallax map.

posts.author: Kes
posts.body:
This is how I've done it.  It works for me, but everyone needs to develop their own best method.
Before doing anything in the editor:
I have to start with at least a broad idea of the story.  Until I have that, I haven't got a clue what I'm going to need to tell this story.
From there, broad idea of the characters to fit the story.
World in which this happens -> the type of maps I'll need.
Broad idea of the general mechanics.
What skills would these particular characters, with their backstory and place in this story, have?
Only when I have those broad ideas - which get changed constantly during development - do I open up RM.

These initial issues are very similar to my current project. The problem is that in the new project, we sometimes lose track of what has already been done within it, since there is no way to measure the amount of configurations made.
And this has a direct impact on the configuration of the default tileset. In other words, when we use it to map, the map is contained within the project and can easily be edited or forgotten.
The advantage of using parallax is in storing the scene. However, I also don't like using a single image. The space in a tileset is large enough to create an entire game. This way, I can use small combinations of images to form specific tilesets, small 256x256 packs with forests, kitchens, bedrooms, streets, etc.
Maker doesn't work well when using large or huge maps. The FPS drops and some image positioning bugs can appear. A sandbox game should establish a base and constantly change the map without map transitions. That's what I'm trying to do now, a single map to distribute screen settings.

posts.author: karusomine
posts.body:
I used to start by writing the story and drawing character portraits, but that was a mistake. At least the drawing part.
It's better to start with mapping, eventing, and filling the database/creating mechanics, which can be done by using only the RTP or any placeholders. Save asset creation and other visual customization for the very end (or at least after you have a good amount of progress).

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
It works like this:
1.  High Concept of the idea.  Establish that.  If you don't know what "High Concept" is, feel free to google it.
2.  Game Design Document.  Everything I want in the game as well as the core tenants of the gameplay and story (or themes, if you will) established.  If you're truly serious about making a game, you will do this step before you even begin work on your project.  The most important reason for doing this is because it will prevent scope creep as well as "designing by the seat of your pants", which means your project will turn out much better than it would otherwise (you know, sort of like studying before a test for a better grade rather than just hoping you did okay on the test when you didn't study at all).
3.  Core gameplay systems designed, implemented, and tested.  Testing for fun as well.  Something can be fun for the first 10 times you do it, but is it still fun the 400th time you do it?  The 10,000th?  You can take a page from Early Bungie here and their "design 30 seconds of fun" philosophy.  It's a good way to approach video games.  If you can design 30 seconds of fun, you can endlessly repeat that, iterate on it, and tweak it to keep providing it.  Part of the Core Gameplay Systems is opening the Database in RPG Maker and putting everything into it that will ever need to be in it (so I don't have to touch this again except for balance tweaks).
4.  Story integration.  I'm a writer, so I've typically been writing a lot of the story alongside all of this stuff, but it doesn't get implemented into the game until I'm comfortable with the gameplay.
5.  Map design tends to fall pretty far down for me since I'm usually crafting the play spaces in regard to the story, rather than the other way around (story says player goes here, so I design this location.  Not, design a location and try to make it fit into the story).
6.  Assets of any kind (music, sprites, tilesets, etcetera) are reserved for "game is completed, time to polish".  I placeholder everything up until that point, because I have no way to know what I will and won't need during the design of the game, but I'll know what I need by the time I'm done.  At which point, it's easy to just pay someone to make what I need.  Besides, this is a good way to save money, especially since there's no guarantee I'll even finish making the game I'm working on, and buying assets for a game has NEVER ONCE motivated or guaranteed I'd finish a project.  This is a good way to avoid "Dragon Hoarding" as a developer.  You know, that stupid Dragon way of thining of "that's cool, let me get that, I can definitely use it!" even though nothing in it is remotely usable in your project.  Avoid the "ooo! Shiny!" aspect of game design.

posts.author: BloodyKun
posts.body:
For my game jam game, well, it was a game jam so I already had a basic idea to go off of for the premise.  But to be honest I’m thinking of new stories, scenarios, and characters all the time, so I guess technically that’s where I typically start.
After that, though, it kind of depends.  At least with this project I’ve done already I didn’t plan to make it all that different from the standard gameplay to be had in RPG Maker.  That and I only used original assets for the main characters and some bosses, so I didn’t bother doing any placeholder stuff either.
One of the projects I’m working on right now has me testing if an idea will actually work in engine, so I’ve definitely got very basic placeholders, all in just one test room of sorts with different things.  Once that’s done I’ll likely plan out any upgrades or traversal mechanics, and then both refine the major plot points as well as mapping and level design simultaneously before I go into balancing stuff and tweaking here or there.  I love to do art so I don’t think I could stop myself between processes, but I know I’ll likely reiterate on designs anyway.  Even so, it’s just a part of my process to have to do that to really feel like they are fleshed out.
The last things I usually think about when planning are sound effects and music, not being good at either of those so much.

Have been making a lot of headway with those things, as most of the problems I happen to have is simply running into a bug and then hyper fixating on it instead of just working on something else.

posts.author: lavendermocha
posts.body:
Mapping is my favorite part of the game dev process, and in my opinion one of most important (at least for the style of game I make), so setting and environment is the most important starting place! I tend to think of places I want to make inside the game and then come up with a story that I think would fit inside them.
My other option, which has become slightly more common in my ideas list the more I make games and more comfortable I get writing characters, I come up with a character and a vague concept for the story and flesh it out by designing the setting.
As a result, tileset and character design/graphics are the most important graphics to me to start with!

posts.author: ISC
posts.body: I always start with a small idea, and if that idea stays in my head for days, then I have to make it happen. The inspiration can come from anything: movies, video games, board games, books, even discussions on forums and dedicated channels. The next phase is planning. I often start with notes and small ideas, which I also share with developers in an Italian RPG Maker community. From this feedback, the embryo of the project is born, which I then develop with a GDD, often accompanied by a spreadsheet to test the values and randomness of the mechanics I have in mind. The next phase is searching for images (sprites, UI, HUD) and useful plugins for the project. The final phase is creating the project, with a map entirely dedicated to tests (or a twin project where I experiment with the more complex mechanics before inserting them into the main project). I start with the mechanics, then move on to game design, and finally the music, which is often RTP because I never manage to finish in time. The last phase is cleanup and QOL improvements.

posts.author: Artille
posts.body:
Isn't the first thing you want to know the type of game you want to create?
Story and mechanics are important, but they kinda depend on the type of game you want to build, say you want to make a game like flappy bird, you might want to know that before writing a 50 page long essay about the character.
That being said, there are no rules for an indie game maker stating in what order what must be done.

posts.author: Timeline_man
posts.body:
The way I do it is pretty.... idiosyncratic?
I start with a vague theme or prompt in conjunction with the type of setting I want to have.
From there, I worldbuild, making nations, history, etc.
Then I use a point in that history as the "current day" (This has a side effect, there's a pretty big chance I have lore that is... entirely pointless for the final product, but oh well)
I figure out what kind of people I want my main cast to be, and figure out what kind of context that means for them.
Then I fully conceptualize who the characters are, so that I can come up with a plot that makes sense for them to interact with
then I make the plot
then I figure out what kinds of "special mechanics" will sell the characters, world, or plot.
then I get to implementation.
